newsitem.title: JAPAN: New Nomura president says his fate to lead broker.
newsitem.headline: New Nomura president says his fate to lead broker.

text.p: The president-designate of Nomura Securities Co Ltd says fate has handed him the task of leading the scandal-tainted brokerage at a critical time in its history.
"I felt like it was destiny. I was surprised (when I was asked to take over as Nomura's president) and I thought fate intervened," Junichi Ujiie told Reuters in an interview.
Last week, Nomura surprised the financial markets when it announced that Ujiie would take over on May 1 as president of Japan's leading brokerage in a sweeping management shake-up.

Current president Masashi Suzuki, who will resign to become chairman without representative rights, had just assumed the post just over one month ago when his predecessor stepped down over a scandal involving payoffs to a corporate racketeer.
Fifteen board members, including five vice-presidents, will also resign their posts to become advisers.
Ujiie reiterated that he would establish a transparent management system based on clear rules.
"I will make an utmost effort to establish a new Nomura," he said.
Financial analysts and even Nomura employees say that Ujiie is the type of young, untainted leader with wide international experience that Nomura needs to help win back public trust.
Ujiie. 51, has a doctorate in economics from the University of Chicago and was appointed president of New York-based Nomura Securities International in 1989.
Besides being chairman of that unit, he was in charge of Nomura's overall American operations between June 1992 and May 1996, and has been a managing director since 1995.
Ujiie said that he is prepared for any harsh repercussions the scandal will have on the brokerage in his first year as president.
"We will strive to post profits (for the current financial year), and it is possible."
However, he admits that Nomura's business this financial year will depend on how hard the Finance Ministry comes down on the brokerage after regulators complete their investigation into the scandal.

Prosecutors and Japan's securities watchdog are investigating Nomura for suspected illegal deals linked to a "sokaiya," a type of racketeer who typically extorts money from firms by threatening to disrupt their shareholders' meetings.
The Finance Ministry is likely to suspend some of Nomura's operations, including stock dealing on its own account, for about three months as punishment for the scandal, market sources have said.
Ujiie said that it would be premature for him to forecast earnings for 1997/98 because business results would also be affected by market conditions which he could not predict.

In the financial year ended March 31, Nomura posted a healthy 35.7 percent year-on-year increase in its parent current profit. In March, however, current profit was about half the usual monthly levels, hit by voluntarily business suspensions by its customers due to the scandal.
Despite the setbacks, Ujiie said he is confident of Nomura's long-term future amid the upcoming "Big Bang" era of financial reforms.
Under the government's Big Bang plan, Japan aims to open up its financial markets by the year 2001 in an effort to catch up with New York and London as a financial centre.
Ujiie said he would put more resources to develop creative, value-added financial products and to strengthen its research to cope with the globalisation of Japanese markets.
"Nomura will clearly change through the Big Bang reforms," he said.
